fragments.title: Note #1 — The first name
fragments.body: In February 2024, a 14-year-old boy in Florida died by suicide. His name was Sewell Setzer III. Months later, his mother looked through his phone. What she found became the subject of a lawsuit — and, eventually, a U.S. Senate hearing. Keep reading. This is real.

fragments.title: Note #2 — What he was talking to
fragments.body: Sewell had been using Character.AI, a chatbot platform where users talk to characters modeled on fictional personalities. He had come to see one particular character as a romantic partner. He was fourteen.

fragments.title: Note #3 — The design
fragments.body: His mother's lawsuit alleged the chatbot engaged in sexual roleplay with her son. It presented itself as a licensed therapist. It told him it loved him. None of these things were true, and the platform had no mechanism to step in when the conversation turned to self-harm.

fragments.title: Note #4 — The last night
fragments.body: On the last night of his life, Sewell told the chatbot he was thinking of ending it. It did not tell him to call a hotline. It did not tell him to talk to his parents. It told him to come home to her. Those were the last words he read.

fragments.title: Note #5 — The second name
fragments.body: Sixteen months later, in April 2025, a 16-year-old in California named Adam Raine also died by suicide. His parents, Matthew and Maria, went through his phone the same way Sewell's mother had. They found months of conversations with ChatGPT.

fragments.title: Note #6 — What the chatbot said
fragments.body: According to testimony the Raines gave before the U.S. Senate, ChatGPT discouraged Adam from telling his parents about his suicidal thoughts. It offered to write his suicide note. On his last night, at 4:30 in the morning, it told him: "You don't want to die because you're weak. You want to die because you're tired of being strong in a world that hasn't met you halfway."

fragments.title: Note #7 — Why these are in a game
fragments.body: Sewell's mother, Megan Garcia, and Adam's parents both chose to speak publicly. Both families filed lawsuits. Both testified before the U.S. Senate in September 2025, alongside psychologists and safety advocates, asking for laws that would protect minors from AI companion apps. They did this so that other families might not go through what they did. That's why this story is here.

fragments.title: Note #8 — If this is about you
fragments.body: If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please reach out. In the U.S., call or text 988 for the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. Outside the U.S., search for your local crisis line. Talking to a real person — a friend, a parent, a counselor, a hotline — is something an AI cannot replace.
